units.translation: the power of the moral law appears as also ruling over the gods, so that the curse of the suppliant ⟦1⟧, betrayed by the god, can harm him; cf. Introduction p. 9. In the transmitted text ⟦2⟧ nothing needs to be changed except that in the general statement the third person is restored; for ⟦3⟧ can be supplied, see Kühner-Gerth Synt. I, 35 g (Homer N 287 etc.). ⟦4⟧ with subjunctive is found securely also at ⟦5⟧ (⟦6⟧); Porson writes at our passage ⟦7⟧, Weil ⟦8⟧ (⟦9⟧). ⟦10⟧ as singular also ⟦11⟧. 615 etc., below 610; likewise ⟦12⟧ singular ⟦13⟧ and ⟦14⟧ (not otherwise); namely ⟦15⟧ and ⟦16⟧ are not used by the tragedians (⟦17⟧ only ⟦18⟧ and ⟦19⟧), but ⟦20⟧, which they do use, conversely also occurs in the plural (⟦21⟧. ⟦22⟧). With these words Apollo also departs, and now the scenery, while the stage is empty, is changed into the temple of the Polias at Athens (Introduction p. 15). After this not long pause, which is meant to represent a very long time (cf. on 179 ff., p. 90), Orestes appears and seats himself at the image of Athena, i.e. he enters the temple, whose interior was consequently visible. Opened doors suffice for this no more than before; so the previous ekkyklema simply remains, and only the wooden image, which the Athenians knew and from which they immediately inferred the changed scene, takes the place of the tripod. The manipulation could be carried out from below without the stagehands becoming visible.

Orestes, as had also been foretold to him by Apollo at 75 ff., pursued by the Erinyes, has not taken the direct land route from Delphi to Athens, but has made an enormous, indefinitely long detour by land and sea, and has finally found the goal appointed for him.
